newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germans' doubts mount over Waigel tax reform bid.
newsitem.headline: Germans' doubts mount over Waigel tax reform bid.

text.p: As Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plans to shake up Germany's tax system take shape, popular confidence that he will meet tax-cutting pledges has hit a new low, a leading polling group said on Wednesday.

Waigel's tax strategy, centrepiece of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's bid for a record fifth election win in 1998, sets a bold target of slicing 30 billion marks ($18.77 billion) off the national tax burden.

But wrangling in Kohl's coalition over income tax cuts and a backroom deal to hike value-added tax to partly offset the cuts have dashed hopes among ordinary Germans that they will win out in the end, the Allensbach institute said.
An Allensbach survey found that 53 percent of Germans thought the reform -- to take effect in 1999 -- would simply redistribute taxes. Only 13 percent actually expected cuts.
"A majority of Germans think that the planned tax reform is above all about raising VAT," the institute's Renate Koecher wrote in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung newspaper.

A tax policy working group chaired by Waigel is due to complete its work next week. It is nearing a compromise on a new income tax model, as well as what use to make of the extra cash from a one-point hike in Germany's 15 percent rate of VAT.
Under two proposals being discussed, the top income tax rate would fall from 53 percent to 39 percent.
Waigel favours a sliding scale starting at 19 percent, down from 26 percent, while coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) support a stepped scheme starting at 10 percent.
Kohl will lead a round of coalition talks on Thursday to thrash out details of the tax package, as well as address plans to reform Germany's struggling compulsory pensions scheme.

Coalition leaders said on Wednesday that they had agreed not to peg the VAT hike directly to plans to lighten Germany's high labour overheads -- seen as one reason for a jobs flight which has pushed German unemployment to a post-war record.

Speaking after a meeting of his Christian Social Union (CSU) party, Waigel told reporters: "We must not bring a VAT increase into play too soon over financing welfare benefits. The pressure to save social security costs must be kept up."

Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who can block some tax measures through their control of the upper house of parliament, have flatly rejected a VAT rise to finance a cut in the top rate of income tax for high earners.

In addition to the VAT increase, coalition proposals to tax life insurance, pensions and jobless benefits, as well as "speculative" profits on share and property dealings have stirred a hostile response from special interest groups.
"The Bonn government has succeeded in destroying any confidence people might have had in the wisdom of the reforms," the heavyweight Handelsblatt daily wrote.
Kohl has said political consultations over the tax plan would last all year -- but Germany may not have the luxury of spending so much time putting its financial house in order.

Handicapped by an unemployment rate of nearly 11 percent and tax revenues falling short of target, Waigel will be hard pushed to cut state borrowing and meet his goal of qualifying this year for planned European monetary union in 1999.

Former Bundesbank President Karl Otto Poehl on Tuesday become the latest pundit to cast doubt on whether Germany can cut its budget deficit below the Maastricht ceiling of three percent of gross domestic product in 1997.

"Without a considerable acceleration of economic growth, Germany will fail to meet the deficit criteria," Poehl said in Paris. He added Bonn's insistence on a strict interpretation of the treaty made the situation "a little ugly".
